Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Education | National ‘Gifted pupils’ exemption is an afterthought’ – NPP on BECE ban Source : Prince Adu-Owusu 26 November 2026 7:42pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
The Co-chair of the New Patriotic Party (NPP) Education Committee, Dr Prince Hamid Armah, has described the Education Minister’s decision to make room for exceptionally gifted pupils under the two-year examination ban as an “afterthought”.
According to him, the provision for gifted learners was introduced only after public criticism of the directive, which initially appeared to impose a blanket restriction on pupils who sit the Basic Education Certificate Examination (BECE) ahead of their scheduled year.
Speaking on JoyFM’s Top Story on Thursday, November 26, Dr Armah said the initial announcement by Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu indicated that every child who sat the examination early would face punishment.
“This is an afterthought. I mean, if you recall the statement that the Ministry made, it was very blanket, and it was to the extent that every child who skips shall be punished,” he said.
He noted that the Ghana Education Service (GES) had subsequently issued a directive to regional and district education officials to ensure the enforcement of the Minister’s instruction.
Dr Armah said the Minister’s subsequent clarification allowing exceptions for exceptionally gifted pupils appeared to have been prompted by public outcry.
“And so, I think as a result of the public outcry, the Minister began to make some concessions. And I can say that it’s an afterthought,” he added.
The Education Minister announced the two-year restriction on November 23, 2026, during the launch of the 2026 National Education Week.
Under the directive, JHS 1 and JHS 2 pupils who sit the BECE ahead of schedule would be barred from taking the examination for two years.
The Minister cited equity, discipline and accurate educational planning as reasons for the measure.
However, Dr Armah maintained that the provision did not address his fundamental concern about the policy, which he considers inappropriate.
“My concern is that the policy is a bad policy. It makes no sense,” he said.
